- If sentiment is consistently 0.00, model tends to overestimate early in the horizon and underestimates later — adjust forecast slope downward after initial spike.
- If sentiment is >0.00 (even low), model often overreacts to recent highs — cap forecast growth after 3–5 consecutive days of rising prices.
- When true outcome shows sharp downward spike after a peak, model often fails to correct — add a downward bias correction of 1–2% for the next 3–5 days post-spike.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows strong mean reversion, reduce forecast slope by 0.5–1.0% per day until price stabilizes.
- For 30-day horizon, if model starts at 64–65 and true outcome exceeds 66 within first 5 days, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day for next 5 days to avoid overestimating “recovery”.
- If sentiment history is all 0.00 and model forecast is rising steadily, check for lag — true outcome often dips 1–2 days after model peak — add 1–2 day lag correction in forecast.
- If true outcome shows strong upward momentum after a low, model often underestimates — increase forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day for next 3–5 days if sentiment is 0.00.
- If model forecast is >68 and true outcome is <66, apply downward bias of 1–2% for next 3–5 days — especially if sentiment is 0.00.
- If sentiment is 0.00 and model forecast is rising >0.5% per day for 3+ days, reduce forecast slope by 0.2–0.5% per day to avoid overshoot.
- If true outcome shows sudden spike after a low, model often fails to catch it — increase forecast by 0.5–1.0% for next 2–3 days if sentiment is 0.00.
